The Mahāvākyopaniṣad:
"May there be auspiciousness through the [recitation of] the *karōṇī* verses"—this is the peace;
it is the section concerning the instruction for the direct experience of the Self.

Then the venerable Brahmā said: "We shall explain the supreme Upaniṣad, which consists of the direct experience of Brahman. It is more secret than the secret; it must not be taught to anyone who is not a pure devotee, who is inward-turned, and who is fully disciplined."

I worship the feet of Rāmacandra, who is the state of liberation without a physical body (vikalebara-kaivalya), whose form is the Great Knowledge (mahāvidyā) that establishes the doctrine of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya).

Indeed, this Mahāvākyopaniṣad, which is a division of the Atharvaveda, stands preeminent by first elucidating that the world is nothing but Brahman— established through the awakening to the impossibility of the existence of a phenomenal universe apart from one's own Self. A commentary on it is now commenced, based on its very brief text.
Not finding a person of superior qualification, Brahmā, manifesting his own experience, said:
"Now" (atha). Why? Because it is "immediate" (aparokṣa). First, he states the secrecy of the Upaniṣad about to be spoken, on account of its esoteric meaning, saying:
"From the secret" (guhyāt). [He says this] for one who has not previously practiced, that is, for one lacking the aforementioned means. Why?

Regarding the phrase "to one who is characterized by *sattva*": the meaning is that it should be taught to one who possesses the state of pure *sattva*, who is turned away from [worldly objects], and who has perfected the means such as service to one's own teacher and the like. || 2 ||
The nature and function of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), as well as how knowledge and ignorance are respectively the causes of bondage and liberation, have been examined.
Knowledge is the dispeller of darkness, while ignorance is the source of darkness. For darkness indeed...
The world, consisting of all infinite beings from the gods down to the immovable plants, appears as the manifestation of the Lord;
it is the sphere of worldly activity involving all desires and actions proclaimed by the entirety of the Vedas. || 4 ||
Regarding the question "What is this Upanishad?", he explains it as follows: "Now" (atha).

Now, following the attainment of the aforementioned means, for one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), the existence of that which is other than oneself—the phenomenal world—is bondage, consisting of the path of engagement (*pravṛttimārga*) based on the notion that it exists; its non-existence is liberation (*mokṣa*), consisting of the path of cessation (*nivṛttimārga*).

Regarding the question "What are the causes of the threefold bondage of saṃsāra and liberation?"—the wheel of knowledge (*vidyācakra*) is the cause of liberation because it brings about the cessation of saṃsāra; the wheel of ignorance (*avidyācakra*), however, is the cause of bondage because it causes saṃsāra to proceed. Both of these exist in the form of the cognition that "saṃsāra exists" or "it does not exist."
Having withdrawn and negated both knowledge and ignorance through the awakening that there is no possibility of any entity other than Brahman, and having realized that Brahman—
established by such negation— is one's own self alone, devoid of any counter-correlate, the wise man, at the very moment of perfect knowledge, [attains liberation].

The statement "one becomes liberated while in the disembodied state" (videhamukta) is the conclusion. Regarding the phrase "the world of the wheel of ignorance" (avidyācakra), he says: "ignorance" (avidyā).

That which does not exist apart from Brahman even throughout the three periods of time is this very ignorance; because the world is perceived as real by means of that [ignorance], it is called the "world of ignorance. That itself is the "portion" (aṃśa); that very portion is the sphere of ignorance (avidyāpada). That alone...

[It is called] *tamaḥ* (darkness) because it conceals its own nature. What is this darkness that conceals its own [nature]? To this he says: "Darkness, indeed... Darkness is the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of bodies; for it is concealed from its own knowledge or in time, and thus it is a body (*śarīra*). That very body is the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is its effect.
From Brahmā down to the stationary objects (sthāvara), because it is the concealment of that Brahman— which is devoid of all counter-correlates—

and because it is conventionally designated as "the phenomenal world" (prapañca), its status as empirical (vyāvahārika) or illusory (prātibhāsika) should be understood either from its appearing only for the duration of its manifestation, or from its mere conventional appearance. What [is the distinction]?
Its empirical nature and its apparent nature are as follows:

as long as one's own ignorance persists, [the world] exists for you as an infinite manifestation of all things, like the infinite space within a jar; however, from the perspective of one's own true knowledge, it is like the empty space of the wind.

"One desiring brothers should sacrifice a white animal; one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā* [offering]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.4.6.1), "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal," and so forth—the entire range of ritual activity for those possessing desires, as proclaimed by all the Vedas, thus becomes a matter of worldly practice. || 4 ||
Through the practice of the science of *haṣa*, there is the manifestation of the Supreme Self;
this Self is not darkness. For knowledge is the sun within the cave, a mass of light to be grasped, and nothing else. This is that sun.

The *haṃsa* (the syllable *haṃsa*) is established through the *ajapā* [mantra] as "Brahman am I" (*brahmāhamasmi*). Having perceived it through the inhalation (*prāṇa*) and exhalation (*apāna*) in both their reverse and natural orders, and having attained that state for a long time,
while meditating upon the *brahmarandhra* within the self consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇātman*), there arises *saccidānanda*.
The Supreme Self manifests. || 6 ||
To this, he says: "This Self is not darkness.

This very Self, which is established through the negation of the phenomenal world of non-Self, is not darkness, because it is nothing other than the supreme light that is non-different from one's own inward light. As long as there is the Self...
It is said that for one desiring liberation, the practice of knowledge must be undertaken; thus he says: "Knowledge indeed.

Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the state of the functions of intellect (*jñāna*), discernment (*vijñāna*), right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), and the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), wherein Brahman—which is devoid of even a scent of anything other than itself—is realized as one's own self alone, free from all counter-correlates. Indeed, this is knowledge.

The "internal sun" (antārāditya) refers to that which culminates in the solar consciousness (cidāditya), which illuminates both the internal and external within the sphere of one's own base ignorance;
thus it is called the "solar consciousness. That alone is the orb of the light of pure consciousness (cinmātra-jyotis-maṇḍala), and its mass of radiance.
Only the knowledge of reality that has as its object Brahman alone, devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa-brahmamātra-gocara-tattvajñāna*), is to be accepted;

for it is the cause of the final direct intuition (*caramasākṣātkāra*) and culminates in Brahman alone. That alone is to be accepted, and not any other knowledge with attributes (*saviśeṣajñāna*) whose object is the lower Brahman (*apara-brahma*).
Because it yields results only after a long delay of time, the meaning is that this [knowledge] should not be accepted by those who are intensely desirous of liberation. || 5 ||

To the question, "What are the means—such as knowledge (*jñāna*), discernment (*vijñāna*), and so forth—which serve as the cause for attaining the realization of the truth that is the means for the manifestation of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) to be reached through such knowledge of reality? he says: "This one... [and so on].
That which is here in the person and that which is there in the sun are one. He who knows thus...
In accordance with such scriptural passages as these, this very Sun, who is within the range of our vision, is Brahman;

for he alone possesses the nature of Brahman when all distinctions inherent in him have ceased. This same Sun, having entered through the door of the eye into the heart, is occupied with the functions of inhalation and exhalation.
By means of the exhalation and inhalation (*prāṇāpāna*) in both reverse and direct order, the *haṃsa* is emitted as "so 'ham" (that am I),
accompanied by a recitation (*japa*) that is innate and effortless. Thus, knowledge and higher realization (*vijñāna*) are produced through the practice of this *ajāpa*.

Alternatively, having attained right knowledge— which is difficult to achieve and requires a long period of time— that wise man [perceives] the ignorance regarding his own nature, which consists of the division between the manifest (vyaṣṭi) and so forth within the threefold Brahman; this ignorance follows the phenomenal world characterized by the unity of the manifest and the unmanifest, and is divided into the various categories of the dual, triple, and quadruple.
When that which consists solely of Brahman— established by the negation of the names, forms, and functions [of the world] and characterized by the absence of any counter-correlate—
is thus meditated upon, then the Supreme Self, who is Being-Consciousness-Bliss established through the awakening to the impossibility of even a trace of suffering, [is realized].
The meaning is that he manifests as his own self alone and becomes absorbed therein.
The nature of the flow of knowledge of reality is like the shoreless ocean, bathed by the thousand-rayed sun;
it is neither meditative absorption (samādhi), nor the perfection of yoga (yogasiddhi), nor the dissolution of the mind (manolaya); it is oneness with Brahman.

7. He who, having created all forms and given names, sits speaking [them], the Sun-like one beyond darkness—he, the Ordainer, who first proclaimed him, he who knows the four quarters as the Wise One (*pravidvān*), becomes immortal in this world by knowing him alone; there is no other way. 8. [The verse continues: "He who knows him as the one who dwells within the heart, the golden-colored, like a smokeless fire, he, having shaken off all evil, attains the highest unity with the Supreme Light. 9. "The god Savitṛ, the lord of all that moves and stands, has sent forth his golden light from the sovereign-lord. 65. "The god Savitṛ, the lord of all that moves
A path exists for traveling. By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice;
those were the first laws (dharmas). They, being of great majesty, attained the heavenly vault where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide. || 9–10 ||

The state of one whose knowledge of reality culminates solely in the Brahman that exists thus is radiant and throbbing, suffused by the Supreme Light-Self which is non-different from the inward illumination— resembling a thousand suns and more— that simultaneously illuminates the infinite quarters of space, like the ocean extending to its furthest shore.

Because it is surrounded and encompassed by the essence of Brahman alone—like one who has crossed the ocean with its waves—it does not dissolve; thus it is called *alāla* because it has the nature of Brahman. Indeed, this state cannot be a mere mental modification (*vṛtti*), nor the perfection of yoga (*yogasiddhi*), nor the dissolution of the mind (*manolaya*); rather, it is the oneness of the inner self (*pratyak*) and Brahman. What more [is there to say]? 7. What more?
Therefore, he says "Āditya" [in the verse] to indicate that unity with the inward-facing Brahman (*pratyag-brahmaikya*).

That which is established through the negation of all attributes arising from the unity of the outward-facing and inward-facing consciousness (*parāk-pratyak-cid-aikya*) is situated beyond the darkness that is distinct from itself.

The sun of consciousness, shining with its light that is rare even at the moments of rising and setting, shines everywhere as the supreme form of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). Having discerned the names and forms belonging to the sphere of ignorance and its effects— which are distinct from Himself— the wise man realizes them to be false.

Having reflected and performed a negation [of the world], one remains proclaiming that "there is nothing whatsoever apart from Brahman"; thus, only that [Brahman] alone remains. "He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself; he who knows it as being thus without seed (nirbīja) becomes himself without seed."

[This is] because of the statement regarding the attainment of the state of Brahman at the very moment of sensation. And thus, the Creator himself previously declared this meaning: "The wise Śakra, whose fame is renowned for his knowledge of Brahman, [said]: 'I am Prāṇa, the self of intelligence,' regarding the four directions beginning with the eastern one, as well as the intermediate directions."

"Venerate him as the immortal part within me"—thus [the teacher says]. But regarding the fruit of knowledge, he declared this meaning: "The knower of Brahman, free from taint and devoid of passion, attains Brahman alone";
knowing the Supreme Self in this way as being merely his own self, which is non-dual and without a counterpart.

According to the Śruti: "At the very moment of realization, one becomes the Supreme Self; at the very moment of knowledge, one is liberated and attains Kaivalya. This bondage arises from ignorance of one's own nature, and liberation comes from knowledge of one's own nature. This alone is the unobstructed path for the sake of reaching liberation.

"Other than the knowledge of Brahman, no other path exists. (9) Thus, even the gods, Indra and the others, having realized Brahman as non-dual, their own self alone— realizing that nothing exists apart from Brahman— worshipped the sacrifice known as Viṣṇu, who is Brahman, by means of the sacrifice of knowledge.

Those who meditate, "I am Brahman," and rejoice while still living are the ones liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). For those who have attained the state of being liberated while living, these were the primary qualities of the gods;
these are the primary qualities of one liberated while living, beginning with humility (*amānitva*) and so forth, as well as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth.
The Pradhānas became their seats. Such is the majesty of the gods:
that celestial realm where the ancient Sādhyas and the hosts of gods dwell as liberated while living (jīvanmukta); having attained that heaven, they shine forth. || 10 ||
The meditation on the light of the breath-flow:
"I am that Sun, the supreme light; the light of the Sun, I am Śiva; the light of the Self, I am Śukra; I am the sustainer of all lights. (11)

(p. 306) Regarding the question, "What do the gods do there?", he says, "So am I," to show that they abide in the practice of contemplating the unity of the inner and outer consciousnesses: "That which is the supreme light, I am that—the sun of consciousness; that which is the light of the sun, I am that—Śiva; that which is I, Śiva, and the light of the sun, I am that—Śukra."

The inner self non-different from the Supreme Self is the essence of all light; thus, through the exchange [of perspectives], I am the Supreme Light non-different from the inner radiance—Om. To the Fourth beyond the Fourth, the Brahman which is the cause of the unity between the inner and outer divisions signified by the syllable Om.
The meaning is that even today they meditate and exert themselves [in this way], thinking: "It is merely our own nature, devoid of any counter-correlate.
This is the fruit of the Haṃsa-jyotis-vidyā taught in the Atharvaśiras; one who studies it in the morning destroys the sin committed during the night.
It removes [evil]. One who recites it in the evening removes the evil committed during the day. Thus, by employing it both in the evening and in the morning, one who is sinful becomes sinless.
One should recite it at midday while facing the sun.
One is liberated from the five great sins and the minor sins; one obtains the merit of having mastered all the Vedas; and one attains union with the Great Viṣṇu—thus says the Upaniṣad. 12.
He states the fruit of this knowledge: "This," etc. What more need be said?
One attains union with the Great Lord Viṣṇu. The word "Upaniṣad" is used here to signify the completion of the Upaniṣad of the Great Sentence (Mahāvākya). || 12 ||
By the Brahmayogin Śrī Vāsudevendra,
this brief commentary on the Mahāvākya Upaniṣad has been written;
the exposition of the Mahāvākyas consists of thirty-two verses in length.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahāvākya Upaniṣad, comprising ninety-two verses, within the commentary on the Ātharvaṇa Upaniṣads, composed by Śrī Rāmadāsa.
